title: MESH-GRIP on ACS Nano: Graphene Microneedle-Mesh Interfaces for 3D Organoid Electrophysiology
excerpt: Our MESH-GRIP platform, published in ACS Nano, addresses the 3D electrophysiology bottleneck highlighted by CNTV's recent coverage of carbon-based biological computing.
body: CNTV (央视网) recently featured a compelling piece on carbon-based biological computers — the on-chip brain-computer interface intelligent interaction system developed by Professor Li Xiaohong's team at Tianjin University's Haihe Laboratory. The coverage highlighted a fundamental bottleneck: how do you reliably record electrical signals from three-dimensional, shape-shifting neural organoids?

This is precisely the challenge our MESH-GRIP platform addresses. Recently published in ACS Nano (DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.5c08827), our work — led by Professor Xingyu Jiang's group at SUSTech with Wu Yan as first author — introduces an elastic thermoplastic polyurethane/graphene microneedle-mesh interface that achieves stable, high-yield electrophysiological recording from neural organoids without damaging their native 3D architecture.

CNTV's coverage brings public attention to a critical challenge in bioelectronics: the gap between the promise of organoid-based computing and the reality of interfacing with living 3D tissue. Our MESH-GRIP is one answer to that challenge.
Why 3D Recording Remains a Bottleneck

Neural organoids — self-organizing 3D tissues derived from pluripotent stem cells — recapitulate key features of brain development and are central to both disease modeling and emerging biocomputing paradigms. However, their irregular, evolving surface morphology makes stable electrical contact extremely difficult. Traditional planar microelectrode arrays (MEAs) require organoids to be pre-adhered for 1–2 weeks, which can alter their 3D neural network architecture. Penetrating probes risk mechanical damage. The field urgently needs interfaces that conform to complex 3D surfaces while preserving tissue integrity.

Key Insight
MESH-GRIP combines elastic microneedles with a stretchable mesh substrate — the microneedles establish gentle contact without penetration damage, while the open mesh preserves media exchange essential for organoid health.
MESH-GRIP: Design and Fabrication
MESH-GRIP (Microneedle Elastic Substrate Hybrid-Graphene Recordable Interfacial Patch) integrates two conductive materials into a single elastomeric platform:

• Graphene microneedles: Conductive TPU/graphene composite needles that conform to the organoid surface, providing intimate electrical contact without tissue penetration.
  • Liquid metal (EGaIn) interconnects: Gallium-indium alloy traces embedded in the mesh, maintaining conductivity under deformation.
  • TPU mesh substrate: A stretchable thermoplastic polyurethane network that supports the organoid while allowing free media exchange.
Fabrication Pipeline
The device is fabricated via a three-step microfluidic patterning approach:

1. Conductive layer preparation: 3D-printed PDMS templates define microneedle cavities and interconnect channels. Graphene paste is vacuum-injected into the microneedle molds, followed by liquid metal ink filling of the circuit channels.
  2. Mesh substrate formation: TPU solution is injected into a mesh-patterned microfluidic channel. After solvent evaporation, the cured TPU film — now embedding the conductive circuitry — is peeled from the template.
  3. Encapsulation and release: Sodium alginate is applied as a sacrificial protective layer over the microneedle tips. PDMS is then used to encapsulate the interconnect regions (leaving tips protected). Finally, the alginate is dissolved in water, exposing the graphene microneedle tips while the interconnects remain insulated.
This approach is low-cost, scalable, and avoids cleanroom-intensive steps such as CVD graphene transfer, photolithography, or Ti/Au metal deposition used in conventional neural probes.
Performance Highlights

• Mechanical resilience: Maintains structural integrity under 200% tensile strain; no liquid metal leakage after 2,000 stretch cycles.
  • Electrical performance: Average impedance of 139.83 kΩ at 1 kHz with excellent channel-to-channel consistency.
  • Recording yield: Over 60% active channel ratio — significantly exceeding the ~40% achieved by commercial planar MEAs under comparable conditions.
  • Signal quality: Spontaneous neural activity recorded at 100–150 μV amplitude with 10–20 dB SNR; glutamate-evoked responses clearly detected.
  • Biocompatibility: Live/dead staining showed no significant difference from conventional low-attachment culture after one week on the device.
Beyond Planar Electrodes

A defining advantage of MESH-GRIP is that it does not require the organoid to be pre-cultured or physically fixed onto the electrode surface. The device's concave geometry guides the organoid into position via gravity alone, and the elastic microneedles establish reliable electrical contact without adhesives, clamps, or tissue penetration. This preserves the organoid's native 3D cytoarchitecture — a prerequisite for physiologically meaningful recordings.

The platform also enabled spatial mapping of neural activity across the organoid surface, revealing electrophysiological "hot spot" regions that would be invisible to sparse or planar electrode configurations.
<hr>

Future directions include integrating the platform with vascularized perfusion systems for long-term chronic recording, increasing electrode density through advanced microfabrication, and extending the approach to assembloids and other multi-region 3D tissue models.
